# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-37 (Extended v239)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to summer Year 10, and 1784-1820 (Marseilles/Pharaon timeline). Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery, Rue Mondétour, Tuileries, Rue Saint-Jacques, Rue de la Jussienne, Rue Coq-Héron, Rue Bussy, Lyons, Grenoble. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven. Marseilles: La Canebière, Rue de Noailles, Allées de Meilhan, Rue du Grand Cours, Rue de l'Homme Armé, Medusa fountain, Palais de Justice, Accoules clock-tower, Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis, La Consigne, Frioul, Pilon, Porto-Ferrajo, Naples, Elba, Island of Elba, Point des Catalans, Ile Ratonneau, Rue de la Loge, Catalans, Madrid, Cape Pharo, Cape de Morgiou, Château d'If. **Timeline: 1814-1820 Marseilles; 1 March 1814 Dantès' arrest; spring Year 10 (1833) current time in English subplot; 30 July 1816 Dantès' prison reckoning.**

## English Subplot Summary (through Chapter 37, spring Year 10)

**Established solemn promises**: Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild fallen wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine promise to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe. Yera Haskick gave Lurald Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Quenford (winter Year 9). Eldest daughter of Lura Haskick kept promise made to Nerine Prydenridge: chapel roof repair at Kelmere completed by harvest (winter Year 9). Fewyn gave Havus Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Salcombe (winter Year 9). Luena gave husband of Yera Stenworth solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Haskick family (winter Year 9). **Sebin swore to youngest daughter of Havus Stenworth to repair roof of chapel at Wilholt** (spring Year 10).

**Chapter 34-35 migrations**: Taric Corrley moved from Dungate to Kelmere with Kassa Stenson. Luena Stenenridge's only son moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth married Sebin Brackick at Torton; couple lived in Torton thereafter. Fewyn Stenworth moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby with Havus. Pelia Lindmere moved to Yarlby with Rorald Lindmere. Havie Prydenridge found work in Staveford, moved there; Isric Thornmere followed her within the month. Youngest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth was apprenticed anew and became a herbalist. Youngest son of Nelan Brackick was apprenticed anew and became a weaver.

**Chapter 36-37 winter/spring scenes and rhythms**: Frost silvered hedges; light went early; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; smoke lay flat over fields; wind carried salt and tar smell; road rutted and puddled after thaw. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Children chased hoop down lane; rain threatened since morning but held off; dog barked at nothing then went quiet; baker's boy late, line at oven grew long. Multiple characters hummed childhood tunes while scrubbing steps (Rovus, Ismira, Isric, Yewyn, Movus). Ismira and Movus fell asleep in chairs before fire caught. Ismira laughed at story nobody else found funny. **RUMOR—Isric Thornmere told Havie Prydenridge old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar.** **RUMOR—In letter Semor Brackick burned after reading, youngest son of Malis Prydenridge revealed old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar.** Movus Brackick bought ribbon at stall and regretted it; counted coins twice, came up penny short. Isric Thornmere won copper chalice from Gadrek Prydenridge at cards fairly. Jotho Thornmere mended torn sleeve. **Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.** Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Movus mended torn sleeve by window, said little. Rorald and Fewyn Stenworth talked of weather, harvest, lame horse. Rorald read almanac aloud, mispronouncing saints. Yewyn Haskick complained of aching back. Salt price repeatedly discussed; Gadrek laughed at story nobody else found funny; Rozek Stenenridge pressed jade mirror into Luvie Prydenridge's hands; Yewyn and Rozek sorted old letters by candlelight; Rorald Lindmere and others sorted letters; Havus fell asleep in chair; Luvie remarked river was up again. **Ismira Stenson died that summer from festering wound; buried at Kelmere.** **Bone compass Ismira owned went to Matho Stenson.** **Son born to Luvie Prydenridge and Semor Brackick, named Brevus Brackick; family lived in Ostcombe.** **Daughter born to Pelde Stenworth and Sebin Brackick, named Elvie Brackick; family lived in Torton.** **Son born to Wenelle Lindmere and Rovus Prydenridge, named Madan Prydenridge; family lived in Kelmere.** Multiple characters asked: "Will it rain, do you think?" (Gadrek to Nerine; Luena to Lurald; Luena to Brevus Brackick; Rovus to Wenelle; Wenelle to Kassa). Yewyn walked long way round to avoid muddy square; Luena Stenenridge walked long way round to avoid muddy square. Febin Prydenridge and Yewyn Corrford talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse. Ilrald Prydenridge and Pelde talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse. Davus remarked salt price is scandal; Elvie Brackick agreed. Pelde Stenworth laughed at story nobody else found funny. Pelde Stenson fell asleep in chair before fire caught. Harine and Davus discussed river being up in spring. **Kadrek Brackick argued with carter over price of sack of oats.** **Rinelle counted coins twice and came up penny short.** **Ilrald counted coins twice and came up penny short.** **Madan Prydenridge counted coins twice and came up penny short.** **Luvie Prydenridge meant to go to Kelmere before frost, but roads flooded and journey put off.** **Brevus told Yera he looked tired; Yera did not deny it.** **Gadrek Prydenridge mended torn sleeve by window and said little.** **Rozek Stenenridge bought ribbon at stall and regretted it.** **Nerine spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight.** **Rozek Stenenridge and Luena talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse.** **Matho laughed at story nobody else found funny.** **Madan Prydenridge walked long way round to avoid muddy square.** **Kassa Stenson spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight.** **Taric Corrley read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half saints.** **Febin Prydenridge packed single trunk and moved from Kelmere to Elmhaven.** **Rovus Prydenridge laughed at story nobody else found funny.** **Madan Prydenridge read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half saints.** **Lurald Stenworth spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight.** **Gadrek bought ribbon at stall and regretted it.** **Yewyn watched clouds and predicted rain, wrongly.** **Madan fell asleep in chair before fire caught.**

## Marseilles/Pharaon Subplot (1814-1820): Dantès' Imprisonment and Escape Tunnel

**Edmond Dantès' arrest (1 March 1814)**: Young sailor Edmond Dantès jumped into skiff at La Canebière. Reported Captain Leclere dead; would become captain with M. Morrel's aid. Captain at twenty, hundred louis pay, share in profits. Wedding feast at La Réserve with Mercédès; betrothal announced. Danglars and Fernand conspired; Danglars wrote denunciation with left hand naming Dantès as Murat's agent carrying letters for usurper. Caderousse read letter, comprehended misery, tried to prevent it but Danglars destroyed it. Magistrate arrived during feast; announced arrest order. Villefort interrogated Dantès; Dantès explained Captain Leclere's death and commission: sailed to Island of Elba, delivered ring, was admitted to grand-marshal, received letter to carry to Paris person—act his captain bade him do. **Villefort destroyed fatal letter—only proof against Dantès.** Mercédès came unobserved to Villefort's door inquiring after Dantès; Villefort pushed by her, closed door. Villefort's remorse seized him; if Renée or Mercédès had pleaded, his cold hands would have signed release, but no voice broke stillness. **The hapless Dantès was doomed.** Villefort fled to Tuileries and audience with King Louis XVIII, reporting conspiracy and sailor's visit to Elba; King praised him and gave Legion of Honor cross. **Noirtier—Villefort's father—disguised himself: cut whiskers, changed cravat, wore dark brown coat, narrow-brimmed hat, took bamboo switch, walked with easy swagger past sentries.**

**Dantès' imprisonment and psychological dissolution (1 March 1814–Year 4+)**: Through Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis to quay, boarded boat to Frioul. Saw light of Point des Catalans where Mercédès dwelt. Black, frowning Château d'If appeared. Jailer placed knee on chest, levelled carbine. Locked in bare underground chamber, lamp on stool. Fragment of plaster: marked 30th July, 1816; made mark daily to avoid losing reckoning. Days passed, weeks, months—expected release in fortnight. Waited three months, then six more, then ten months and a half. At end of first year, governor transferred; new governor learned prisoners' numbers instead of names. Edmond became number 34. Nearly four years passed; at end of second year ceased marking time. Sustained by pride of conscious innocence; then doubted own innocence; then supplicated man, not God. Asked for companion, even mad abbé—refused. Exhausted human resources, turned to God; recollected mother's prayers. Yet remained prisoner. Gloom settled heavily. Rage supplanted religious fervor; blasphemies made jailer recoil; dashed against walls. Consigned persecutors to horrible tortures insufficient because after torture came death. Contemplation of yawning abyss offered strange consolation.

**Starvation resolve and renewal through mysterious sound**: "I wish to die," resolved Dantès. Chose starvation method; swore oath to die. Cast out food twice daily through barred aperture. Hunger made food acceptable; held plate hour at time, gazed at morsel. Young—only four or five-and-twenty—had nearly fifty years to live. What unforeseen events might not open prison door? Yet thought of oath, would not break it. Persisted until had not strength to rise and cast supper out. Next morning could not see or hear; hoped he was dying. Felt stupor creeping over, bringing almost contentment; gnawing pain ceased; thirst abated. Saw myriads of lights dancing—twilight of country called Death. Heard continual scratching as if made by huge claw, powerful tooth, or iron instrument attacking stones. Brain responded to liberty! Heaven had taken pity, sent this noise as warning on brink of abyss. Perhaps beloved one was thinking of him, striving to diminish distance. For week since resolving to die, during four days carrying out purpose, had not spoken to attendant. Now jailer might hear noise and destroy ray of hope soothing his last moments. Jailer brought breakfast. Dantès raised himself, began talking about everything—bad food, coldness, grumbling—to excuse speaking louder, weary jailer's patience, who brought broth and white bread. Dantès drank contents with indescribable pleasure. Did not wish to die.

**Tunnel work begins (continuing Year 4+)**: At night Dantès heard subterranean workman mining way. Day came, jailer entered. Dantès said jug fell from hands while drinking; jailer fetched another without removing fragments. **Listened until steps died away, hastily displaced bed, saw by faint light he had labored uselessly attacking stone instead of removing plaster surrounding it. Damp rendered plaster friable; broke off in small morsels. In half hour scraped handful. Mathematician might calculate that in two years, supposing rock not encountered, passage twenty feet long and two feet broad might form.** Broke three sharp fragments, concealed in bed, left rest on floor. **Jug breaking too natural accident to excite suspicion.** Worked three days removing cement, exposing stonework. Wall built of rough stones; hewn stone blocks imbedded at intervals for strength. Uncovered one, must remove from socket. **Jailer accustomed to pour soup contents into Dantès' plate; Dantès washed plate after eating with wooden spoon. Evening Dantès put plate on ground near door; jailer stepped on it and broke it. "You destroy everything... I shall leave you saucepan, pour soup into that."** Dantès beside himself with joy, rapidly devoured food, waited hour, removed bed, took saucepan handle, inserted point between hewn stone and rough stones, employed as lever. Slight oscillation showed all went well. Hour's work extricated stone, leaving cavity foot and half in diameter. Carefully collected plaster, carried to corner, covered with earth. **Continued work without ceasing.** At dawn replaced stone, pushed bed against wall, lay down. **Raised eyes to heaven, clasped hands beneath coverlet. Felt more gratitude for piece of iron than anything. Prisoner on other side ceased labor; no matter—greater reason for proceeding. If neighbor would not come, he would go to neighbor.** **All day toiled untiringly; by evening extracted ten handfuls plaster and stone fragments.** When jailer's visit arrived, straightened saucepan handle, placed in accustomed place. Turnkey poured ration of soup and fish—thrice a week prisoners deprived of meat. **Noted prisoner on other side had ceased labor.**

## Marius and Cosette: Courtship to Death Vigil

**Spring Year 6 confessions through barricade**: Marius revealed orphan status, lawyer profession, father colonel-hero. Cosette revealed convent upbringing, dead mother, father M. Fauchelevent. Éponine died leading Marius to barricade. Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed. Shot broke collar bone. Vigorous hand seized him before consciousness vanished.

**Medical recovery and wedding (1 February 1833)**: Doctor declared recovery assured. Learned Cosette was not daughter of old man she called father; another Fauchelevent was real father. Dowry: five hundred eighty thousand francs, constituted legacy by dead person desiring to remain unknown. **Wedding at church of Saint-Paul: Cosette wore white taffeta petticoat, Binche guipure robe, English point veil, pearl necklace, orange flower wreath. Route: Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. Jean Valjean rose, left unperceived during celebration.**

**Javert's death and estrangement**: Javert drowned in Seine. **RUMOR—Marius suspects Jean Valjean killed Javert in barricade.**

**Jean Valjean's revelation and withdrawal**: **Proclaimed: "I am an ex-convict."** Marius shocked, concluded Jean Valjean horrible workman but admirable work. Address changed to _you_, "Madame," "Monsieur Jean." Cosette became more gay, less tender. One day chanced to say "father." "Say Jean"—She replied: "Ah! truly, Monsieur Jean." Complete extinction ensued. Neatly clad in black, emerged daily at same hour towards nightfall from Rue de l'Homme Armé. **He was eighty years old; before Marius' marriage, would have hardly been taken for fifty; that year had counted for thirty.** Later confined to apartment, then bed. **Revealed black jet from England, white jet from Norway; invented way of substituting slides; six hundred thousand francs made. Also managed very well with glass goods. Adjured Marius: "Have no fear, the six hundred thousand francs really belong to Cosette!"** **[Heard by God alone]: "All is over. I shall never see her more... What is frightful is to die without seeing her."** Final decline: breath intermittent; difficulty moving forearm; feet lost all movement. As wretchedness of limb increased, all majesty of soul displayed. Light of unknown world visible in eyes. **In cemetery of Père-Lachaise, vicinity of common grave, far from elegant quarter, in deserted corner beside old wall, beneath great yew tree over which climbs wild convolvulus, amid dandelions and mosses, lies stone.**

## Thénardier's Blackmail and Marius's Confrontation

**Thénardier's discovery and exposure**: Through daughter Azelma tracking married pair, discovered Cosette was Madame la Baronne Pontmercy. **Offered to drive individual from family who has no right there; claimed twenty thousand francs as price.** **Wore black cloth coat, silk waistcoat, boots, green glasses, plastered gray hair. With agility of monkey, tore off spectacles, withdrew two quills from nose, took off face as man takes off hat.**

**Marius's confrontation and evidence**: Revealed Javert's suicide facts announced in _Moniteur_ 15th June, 1832: Javert reported to prefect that, having been taken prisoner in barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie, he owed his life to magnanimity of insurgent who, holding him under pistol, fired into air instead of blowing out his brains. **Marius possessed evidence, certain date, irrefragable proof. "You are an infamous wretch! you are a liar, a calumniator, a villain... you have only succeeded in glorifying him. And it is you who are the thief! And it is you who are the assassin! I saw you, Thénardier Jondrette, in that lair on the Rue de l'Hôpital."** Offered twenty thousand francs total, ordered him to America with daughter; wife dead. **The moral wretchedness of Thénardier was irremediable. He was in America what he had been in Europe. With Marius' money, Thénardier set up as slave-dealer.**
